title: Choosing a Name for Your Computer
summary: A republished Communications of the ACM article offering guidelines on what to do and what not to do when naming your computer. It is FYI 5 and informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC offers advice for choosing names for computers. It recommends names that are easy to say, spell, and remember, and warns that names tied to a person or temporary project can cause confusion later.

questions: how do i choose a computer name
subtitle: Practical guidelines for choosing computer names people can remember and use.

tldr.problem: Poorly chosen computer names can be confusing to say, spell, remember, or keep when a machine's role changes.
tldr.mechanism: The essay recommends short, familiar, distinctive names and explains common naming pitfalls with examples.
tldr.outcome: This FYI memo republishes naming advice; it does not specify a technical standard.

today: RFC 1178 is an informational FYI memo that republishes computer-naming advice. It does not define a technical standard.

sections.title: Why Computer Names Matter
sections.content:
People need to distinguish computers when they talk about them, and computers also use names when exchanging information. The essay focuses on choosing names that are clear to people, rather than on how a name is resolved by software.

The author draws on examples of naming problems to explain why a name that seems clever at first can become inconvenient as machines and their uses change.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer name should help people identify the machine without causing confusion. This essay is about choosing the name, not about how network software looks it up.

sections.title: Names That Create Confusion
sections.content:
The essay advises against using ordinary words that already have a meaning in conversation, a person's name, or a name tied to one project. Such names can become ambiguous or stop fitting when a computer changes tasks or ownership.

It also recommends avoiding long names, unusual spellings, domain names, domain-like names, embarrassing words, names that begin with digits, punctuation, and a dependence on uppercase and lowercase distinctions.
sections.plainLanguage: Avoid names that sound like ordinary instructions or identify a person or temporary job. Choose a spelling and form that people can say and type without special explanation.

sections.title: Choosing Names That Work Well
sections.content:
The essay suggests using uncommon real words and a shared theme for a group of computers. A theme can make names feel related while leaving room to add more machines.

It says that a computer's name is an identifying label, not a reliable description of what the computer does. A locally reasonable name usually does not need to be unique across every other domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Use memorable words that are unlikely to be confused with everyday conversation. A theme can help name a group, but the name should not promise that the machine will always have one job.

sections.title: Names Are Costly to Change
sections.content:
The author notes that renaming a computer can take more work than expected because software, records, and people may continue to use its old name. Choosing carefully at the start can save effort for users and administrators.

RFC 1178 republishes an essay that first appeared in the Communications of the ACM. The memo identifies itself as FYI 5 and says it does not specify a standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Choose a name with future changes in mind, because old references can be hard to find and update. The RFC is informational guidance, not a naming protocol.

references.text: Mockapetris, P., "Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities", RFC 1034, November 1987.
